retrieved_context.question_title: How to extract just plain text from .doc & .docx files?
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Here is the simplest possible Java code for converting a .doc or .docx document to plain text:

import java.io.FileInputStream;
import java.io.FileWriter;
import java.io.IOException;

import org.apache.poi.POITextExtractor;
import org.apache.poi.extractor.ExtractorFactory;
import org.apache.poi.openxml4j.exceptions.OpenXML4JException;
import org.apache.xmlbeans.XmlException;

public class WordToTextConverter {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            convertWordToText(args[0], args[1]);
        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException aiobe) {
            System.out.println("Usage: java WordToTextConverter <word_file> <text_file>");
        }
    }

    public static void convertWordToText(String src, String desc) {
        try {
            FileInputStream fs = new FileInputStream(src);
            final POITextExtractor extractor = ExtractorFactory.createExtractor(fs);
            FileWriter fw = new FileWriter(desc);
            fw.write(extractor.getText());
            fw.flush();
            fs.close();
            fw.close();

        } catch (IOException | OpenXML4JException | XmlException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
    }
}

retrieved_context.question_title: List reverse Ocaml
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: List reverse Ocaml A:

The error is telling you that support tl has type 'a list while the :: operator works like this: 1 :: [2;3] = [1;2;3]. Conceptually what you are trying to do is [3; 2] :: 1, which is not how the operator works.

If you want to append hd at the end of a list you need to use the @ operator (or the append function):

let reverse list_ =
  let rec support list_ =
    match list_ with
    | [] -> []
    | hd :: tl -> support tl @ [hd] in
  let return = support list_ in return

Now the problem is time complexity, we are iterating through the entire list for each element. To deal with this we can use a list on which we accumulate the elements:

let reverse list =
  let rec support acc list_ =
    match list_ with
    | [] -> acc
    | hd :: tl -> support (hd :: acc) tl in
  let return = support [] list in return

This code could be rewritten a bit considering that:

  • the expression let return = support [] list in return is the same as support [] list</

title: How to Practically Ship GLSL Shaders with your C++ Software
ground_truth_answer:
There is just "store them directly in the executable" or "store them in (a) separate file(s)", with nothing in-between. If you want a self-contained executable, putting them into the binary is a good idea. Note that you can add them as resources or tweak your build system to embed the shader strings from separate development files into source files to make development easier (with the possible addition of being able to directly load the separate files in development builds).

Why do you think shipping the shader sources would be a problem? There is simply no other way in the GL. The precompiled binaries are only useful for caching the compilation results on the target machine. With the fast advances of GPU technology, and changing GPU architectures, and different vendors with totally incompatible ISAs, precompiled shader binaries do not make sense at all.

Note that putting your shader sources in the executeable does not "protect" them, even if you encrypt them. A user can still hook into the GL library and intercept the sources you specify to the GL. And the GL debuggers out there do exactly that.

UPDATE 2016

At SIGGRAPH 2016, the OpenGL Architecture Review Board released the GL_ARB_gl_spirv extension. This will allow a GL inmplementation to use the SPIRV binary intermediate language. This has some potential benefits:

  1. Shaders can be pre-"compiled" offline (the final compilation for the target GPU still happens by the driver later). You don't have to ship the shader source code, but only the binary intermediate representation.
  2. There is one standard compiler frontend (glslang) which does the parsing, so differences between the parsers of different implementations can be eliminated.
  3. More shader languages can be added, without the need to change the GL implementations.
  4. It somewhat increases portability to vulkan.

With that scheme, GL is becoming more similar to D3D and Vulkan in that regard. However, it doesn't change the greater picture. The SPIRV bytecode can still be intercepted, disassembled and decompiled. It does make reverse-engineering a little bit harder, but not by much actually. In a shader, you usually can't afford extensive obfuscuation measures, since that dramatically reduces performance - which is contrary to what the shaders are for.

Also keep in mind that this extension is not widely available right now (autumn 2016). And Apple has stopped supporting GL after 4.1, so this extension will probably never come to OSX.

MINOR UPDATE 2017

GL_ARB_gl_spirv is now official core feature of OpenGL 4.6, so that we can expect growing adoption rate for this feature, but it doesn't change the bigger picture by much.

retrieved_context.question_title: Optimize GLSL for half float
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: Optimize GLSL for half float A:

While GLSL does not have a half type, it does have precision qualifiers whose effects are exclusive-to and dependent-on mobile platforms. I'm assuming that the (complete) optimized shader code from your example contains a default qualifier setting floats to mediump like so: precision mediump float; Note though that the actual precision remains unspecified, a mediump float might have 16 bits on one platform while it has 24 bits on another.

Here's the catch though: As stated in the linked article and the GLSL specification precision qualifiers are only supported for portability and ought to have no effect on desktop platforms. That means that even desktop GPUs with float16 support would break with the specification if they honored the precision qualifier. On desktop platforms you'll have to enable and use the appropriate extension(e.g. GL_AMD_gpu_shader_half_float) and its specific syntax(e.g. types) to utilize the float16 capabilities.

GLSL Half (floating point) attribute type
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: GLSL Half (floating point) attribute type A:

OpenGL and OpenGL ES define two concurrent types of precision.

  • Storage precision in buffers
  • Minimum computational precision used in shaders.

Storage precision is defined by your vertex attribute upload, such as GL_FLOAT or GL_HALF_FLOAT. This will be the precision used to store the data in memory.

Usage precision is defined in the shader as highp (at least 32-bit), mediump (at least 16-bit), and lowp (at least 9-bit). These are minimum precisions; it is perfectly legal for a shader to specify a variable as mediump and for the shader compiler to generate fp32 data types. Desktop GPUs tend to only support fp32 computation, so the use of highp, mediump and lowp all map to fp32 data types (the precision qualifiers are only included to keep compatibility with OpenGL ES shaders, and can legally be ignored by the compiler). Mobile GPUs implementing OpenGL ES tend to map highp to fp32, and mediump and lowp to fp16. Detailed information can be found in the GLSL ES 3.0 Specification, Section 4.5.1

To address the challenge of debugging a native Win32 application like `explorer.exe` without access to its source code, while seeking a graphical debugger that supports Microsoft's symbol server, here are some options and solutions:

### Options for Graphical Debuggers

1. **Visual Studio with Debugging Tools for Windows**:
   - Although primarily known for application development, Visual Studio includes capabilities to debug native Win32 applications. You can configure it to use the Microsoft symbol server:
     - Open Visual Studio.
     - Go to **Tools > Options**.
     - Under **Debugging > Symbols**, add the Microsoft Symbol Server (`http://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols`).
     - To debug `explorer.exe`, you can attach to its process via **Debug > Attach to Process**.

2. **x64dbg**:
   - This is a newer, open-source graphical debugger that supports debugging both 32-bit and 64-bit applications. It has good support for symbols, and the community is active in adding features.
   - You can download it from [x64dbg](https://x64dbg.com). After starting the application, you can load `explorer.exe` and configure symbol loading through the Symbol Server settings.

3. **WinDbg Preview**:
   - While WinDbg is traditionally command-line, WinDbg Preview introduces a more user-friendly GUI. It supports symbols and provides many powerful debugging features. You can enable symbols using the symbol server similarly to the method described for Visual Studio.
   - Download it from the Microsoft Store.

4. **Radare2 with Cutter**:
   - Radare2 is a command-line utility, but Cutter is a graphical frontend for it. While not as straightforward as Visual Studio, it offers symbol support and is quite powerful for reverse engineering and debugging.
   - You can find both tools on the [Cutter GitHub page](https://github.com/radareorg/cutter).

### Steps to Debug `explorer.exe`

1. **Configure Symbol Settings**:
   - For any debugger you choose (Visual Studio, x64dbg, WinDbg Preview), ensure that the Microsoft Symbol Server is added as a source for symbols.

2. **Start Your Debugger**:
   - Open your chosen debugger and load or attach to the `explorer.exe` process.
   - In cases where you need to attach, you can find `explorer.exe` in the list of running processes.

3. **Setting Breakpoints and stepping through the code**:
   - Once attached, you can set breakpoints and step through the instructions to debug as you would in a development environment. The use of symbols will enable you to see function names and variable names, which makes it easier to understand the code's flow.

4. **Analyze Crash Dumps**:
   - If `explorer.exe` crashes, you can analyze it with these debuggers. Loading a crash dump allows you to determine what was happening at the time of the crash and is particularly useful for identifying issues in large applications without source code.

### Conclusion

While standalone graphical debuggers with symbol server support are somewhat rare, the options above provide capabilities to debug `explorer.exe`. It's essential to familiarize yourself with the chosen tool's interface and debugging features for effective investigation of the application.

title: What characters are widely supported in CSS class names?
ground_truth_answer:
Note that class names are defined by HTML, not CSS. HTML4 says the class attribute is a cdata-list, which is space-separated tokens. So a single classname token can contain any character except the whitespace characters.

I wonder what browsers properly understands a slash (/) in a class name, and what browsers support class names starting with a number.

To refer to such names in a CSS class selector you would need to use an escape. eg.:

<div class="1blah/bläh">

is matched by:

.\31 blah\2F bläh { ... }

This is supported by all current browsers. It wasn't supported by IE5, but that's thankfully no longer a concern. (If you had concerns about character encoding mismatches, you might prefer to encode the ä as \E4, but that's not a limitation of CSS as such.)

If you're asking which browsers will let you get away with the invalid selector

.1blah/bläh

Then, well, who cares really? Just use the valid one.

Is there any meaningful difference between using the HTML-encoded vs non encoded characters?

Not in terms of the browser being able to display them in general. If you want to use these as you call them "non-standard" characters (which are very much standard characters, just not ASCII characters), you should specify an encoding, preferably utf-8. The HTML5 way of doing this (which is backwards compatible and supported by pretty much all browsers) is

That said, some tools compiling static HTML from markdown etc. might have problems with it, but that depends on the tool. You're safer using the entities like © there; which you can also always use without specifying an encoding.

llm_answer:
In HTML and CSS, class names are subject to specific restrictions related to the characters that can be used. According to the CSS specification, the following rules apply to class names: 1. **Valid Characters**: - Class names can include letters (`a-z`, `A-Z`), digits (`0-9`), hyphens (`-`), underscores (`_`), and certain special characters (though these should generally be escaped). - A class name must start with a letter (a-z or A-Z) or an underscore (_). It cannot start with a digit (0-9). 2. **Invalid Characters**: - Characters like spaces, slashes (`/`), special symbols (except for `-`, `_`, and letters), and starting a name with a number are not valid in the context of CSS class names. 3. **Practical Browser Support**: - While many modern browsers are quite forgiving with their parsing and can handle certain non-standard practices, using unconventional characters like slashes (/) or starting class names with a number can lead to inconsistencies and unexpected behavior. In JSF, especially when dealing with components like `<h:dataTable>` inside iterative components like `<ui:repeat>`, you might face issues with component IDs and AJAX rendering. The problem you’re facing (unknown ID after adding `ui:repeat`) typically arises from how JSF builds component trees and IDs dynamically.

### Understanding the Issue:
1. **Dynamic IDs**: When you use `<ui:repeat>`, JSF creates a new component instance for each iteration. This affects the ID structure and can lead to mismatches because the component IDs change with each iteration.
2. **Component Context**: AJAX rendering in JSF looks for a specific component tree structure. If the component is not found either due to scope issues or incorrect paths, you get the "unknown id" error.

### Solutions to Access Parent Components:
To resolve the ID issue and correctly reference parent components, consider the following approaches:

1. **Using `@this` and `@form`**: These keywords refer to the current component and the entire form, respectively. For example, you can modify your AJAX rendering target:

   ```xml
   <h:commandButton value="Click me to update" >
       <f:ajax render="@form" />
   </h:commandButton>
   ```

   This renders the entire form, which might be simpler than trying to reference specific IDs, especially in a nested structure.

2. **Referring Using the Client ID**: If you want to refer to the specific parent component within the scope of the dataTable, consider using `clientId` properly. In your case, the hierarchy would look like this:

   ```xml
   <h:commandButton value="Click me to update (#{component.clientId})">
       <f:ajax render=":#{component.parent.clientId}" />
   </h:commandButton>
   ```

   Replace `component.parent` depending on how deeply nested your components are.

3. **Avoid Deep Nesting**: Sometimes, a solution to complex component interaction is to flatten the structure. If feasible, avoid excessive wrapping of UI components in your JSF page. Consider if you can keep the dataTable inside a simpler structure, which helps maintain predictability around component IDs.

4. **Use `ui:include` for Dynamic Content**: If you are able to separate the logic or data, use the `ui:include` tag which allows you to modularize your components. This allows better control over IDs and behavior. 

### Example Code Adjustments:
Following your original code example, you can try something like the following, assuming you want to avoid deep referencing issues:

```xml
<h:form id="wrapperForm">
    <ui:repeat id="blocksRepeat" var="block" value="#{bean.blocks}">
        <h:panelGroup id="rowsWrapper">
            <h:dataTable id="rowsTable" value="#{block.rows}" var="row">
                <h:column>
                    <h:commandButton value="Click me to update">
                        <f:ajax render="@form" />
                    </h:commandButton>
                </h:column>
            </h:dataTable>
        </h:panelGroup>
    </ui:repeat>
</h:form>
```

This modification emphasizes rendering the form directly, removing the complexity around attempting to reference inner components explicitly.

### Closing Thoughts
Whenever you are dealing with nested components in JSF, keeping track of the component tree and how IDs are generated is vital. You can often simplify the design or leverage JSF's built-in keywords to handle most scenarios without needing to access the parent component IDs directly.

llm_answer:
The issue you're facing revolves around integrating OCaml, specifically using the `ocamljava` compiler to generate Java bytecode, while also needing to call C functions. In this context, it's important to clarify how `ocamljava` operates and what limitations it may have regarding calling C functions.

### Background

1. **ocamljava**: This is a compiler that allows you to compile OCaml code to Java bytecode. It's designed to enable some interoperability between OCaml and Java, but it's important to note that it might not support all features available in native OCaml, particularly those that involve low-level C interactions.

2. **Call to C from OCaml**: In native OCaml, you can define functions in C and call them back into OCaml using the Foreign Function Interface (FFI). This is typically done using `ocamlc` or `ocamlopt`, which can link C libraries into OCaml programs, providing the necessary runtime support and callbacks.

### The Problem

You stated that `ocamljava` does not support callbacks into C code from OCaml when compiling to Java bytecode. This is likely accurate; `ocamljava` is primarily focused on converting OCaml constructs to Java constructs and may not retain the C interoperability features of OCaml.

### Possible Solutions

1. **Java Native Interface (JNI)**:
   - Java has a well-defined interface for calling native methods written in C/C++, known as the Java Native Interface (JNI). If you can wrap your C functions in a Java interface using JNI, you may be able to call these functions from your Java bytecode generated by `ocamljava`. 
   - This involves writing Java methods that declare native, using `native` keyword and then providing C code that implements these methods. 
   - The process can be intricate as you'll need to manage the bridging between the Java and C environments yourself. 

2. **Using an Intermediate Wrapper**:
   - You could create a separate OCaml module that utilizes the usual OCaml-C FFI, then compile that module with normal OCaml tools to generate a native executable or library. 
   - You would then create an interface in your Java code to interact with this compiled OCaml code. This requires managing the interactions between the two separately instead of a smooth integration within `ocamljava`.

3. **Consider Other Libraries**: 
   - Evaluate if there are libraries in either Java or OCaml that offer the functionality you need. It might be possible to stay entirely within Java or OCaml without needing C at all.

4. **Re-Implementing Functions**: 
   - In case the above methods are not suitable, consider re-implementing critical functions from your OCaml library in Java. This may not be ideal due to code duplication but is sometimes simpler than dealing with mixed-language complexities.

### Conclusion

In conclusion, due to the limitations of `ocamljava`, you may need to rely on JNI to bridge OCaml and C functionality indirectly through Java, create an intermediate OCaml module that you compile separately, or access equivalent libraries in Java to avoid unnecessary complexity. Each approach has trade-offs, so you'll need to consider your project requirements and choose what's best for your setup.

Q: Format Java 8 LocalDateTime in angularJs view A:

The issue is that by default Jackson doesn't know how to properly serialize the Java 8 date structures (JSR 310) to JSON. As a result, it returns an entire object structure containing dayOfMonth, dayOfWeek, ... as you observed.

A solution would be to serialize your dates to a well-known format, like an ISO-8601 string. To do this, you first have to add support for these Java 8 types by adding the following dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.datatype</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-datatype-jsr310</artifactId>
</dependency>

After that, you should notice that your date is being serialized as an array, for example:

[2019, 2, 8, 11, 0, 0, 0, 0]

This is an array containing the year, month day of the month and so on. However, the AngularJS date filter cannot use these results yet. The proper solution would be to format them as an ISO-8601 string without timezone (considering it's a LocalDateTime). You can do this by disabling the WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS serialization feature within Jackson, by configuring the following property within application.properties:

spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false

ground_truth_answer:

My particular issue was that the project was already using the spring-boot-starter-mail dependency, which includes the com.sun.mail jar. So I had to exclude that from my Maven dependency. <dependency>
    <groupId>com.sun.mail</groupId>
    <artifactId>javax.mail</artifactId>
    <version>1.5.6</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-mail</artifactId>
    <exclusions>

            <groupId>com.sun.mail</groupId>

retrieved_context.question_title: nesting python list comprehensions to construct a list of lists
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: nesting python list comprehensions to construct a list of lists A:

The only really significant difference between strings and lists of characters is that strings are immutable. You can iterate over and slice strings just as you would lists. And it's much more convenient to handle strings as strings, since they support string methods and lists don't.

So for most applications, I wouldn't bother converting the items in data to a list; I'd just do:

data = [line.strip() for line in open(filename, 'r')]

When I needed to manipulate strings in data as mutable lists, I'd use list to convert them, and join to put them back, e.g.:

data[2] = ''.join(sorted(list(data[2])))

Of course, if all you're going to do with these strings is modify them, then go ahead, store them as lists.

retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: Python UnpicklingError: invalid load key, '\xef' A:

Your code works, I will not comment on that. There are other comments that already suggest improvements.

The error you're encountering is not due to the logic, but rather due to how the file was saved or modified afterward.

The error message suggests that the file contains unexpected bytes at the beginning, specifically the UTF-8 BOM (Byte Order Mark). This can happen if:

  • You opened employee-data.csv in a text editor (like Notepad or Excel), and

  • The editor silently saved the file with a different encoding - typically UTF-8 with BOM.

When this happens, the first few bytes of the file (\xef\xbb\xbf) are not valid in the context of a binary pickle stream, hence the UnpicklingError.

Try to save the file in a different format (e.g. ANSI) or regenerate the file without opening it before loading it again.

retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: What are disadvantages to using immutable state in React? A:
  1. Documentation. Some of the most voted questions/rants in SO are about trivial things like updating nested list items all because the documentation is more oriented towards an audience familiar with functional programming, which makes it less approachable to the rest.
  2. Its not trivial to separate the model hierarchy knowledge from your components. I hate to do a this.state.getIn("[parent, child, index]") in a component because it increases the possibility of a model change breaking the component code. This is preventable by extensibility (more on that below) or through helper methods, but you certainly lose the simplicity of plain JS members.
  3. A significant challenge I faced was to be able to serialize and de-serialize the state. The fromJS method supports custom revivers but they are a pita and require careful testing and maintenance.
  4. The Record type is severely stunted by a debilitation called nesting. This is sad because it allows easier (in relative terms) extensibility, but encourages only a single level hierarchy. You cannot easily create nested records from JSON. This makes it difficult to mix them with regular immutable fromJS usage unless you use the above mentioned pita revivers. And did I mention how sad that is, given Records expose model properties as first class members, ensure model integrity and defaults.

title: Node FTP doesn't execute `once('close')` callback when downloading file is large
ground_truth_answer:
This code might give you idea how to handle this in a bit hacky way.

Basically this method allows you to download file from FTP server and save it to local filesystem. It outputs current progress complete_percentage% (current/total) in a single line. Upon finish, it resolves promise, returns path to local file, the same one that you passed as param. 

/**
   * @name downloadFile
   * @desc downloads file from FTP server
   * @param  params, Object of params
   *   @prop auth: object, or null, authorization params
   *   @prop targetedFile: {String} filename e.g. data.txt
   *   @prop localDir: {String} filename on local disk
   *   @prop state: {Object} fileinfo object, {Int} .fileSize property is required
   * @return Promise, resolves given localDir
   */
  downloadFile: params => {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      // validate param types
      if(typeof params.auth !== 'object'
      || typeof params.targetedFile !== 'string'
      || typeof params.localDir !== 'string'
      || typeof params.state !== 'object'
      || typeof params.state.fileSize !== 'number'
      ) throw new Error('You are either missing properties or passed wrong types')

      // initialize
      let ftpClient = new FTP()
      let total = params.state.fileSize
      let progress = 0

      //
      ftpClient.on('ready', _ => {
        console.log(`Downloading ${params.targetedFile} ...`)
        // get file
        ftpClient.get(params.targetedFile, (err, stream) => {
          if (err){
            ftpClient.end()
            return reject(err)
          }

          // upon data receive
          stream.on('data', buffer => {
            progress += buffer.length
            // if progress is complete
            if(progress === total){
              // start checking if local filesize matches server filesize
              let interval = setInterval(_ => {
                if(fs.statSync(params.localDir).size === total){
                  console.log(`Downloading file complete. Location: ${params.localDir}`);
                  clearInterval(interval)
                  ftpClient.end()
                  resolve(params.localDir)
                }
              })
            }
            // show current progress in percentages and bytes
            process.stdout.write(`Progress: ${(progress/total*100).toFixed(2)}% (${progress}/${total})  \r`)
          })
          // pipe writestream to filesystem to write these bytes
          stream.pipe(fs.createWriteStream(params.localDir))
        })
      })
      ftpClient.connect(params.auth)
    })//promise
  }

retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: Why would a node http client request occasionally error out with "socket hang up" after approximately 5 seconds? A:

I seem to have solved this by making two changes to my client code:

  1. As suggested by @HeikoTheißen in comments, I added the following to my axios config to limit the number of sockets per process.
httpAgent: new http.Agent({maxSockets: 10}),
httpsAgent: new https.Agent({maxSockets: 10})
  1. I used the axios-retry package to retry any write requests that failed due to network errors. I used retryCondition: axiosRetry.isNetworkError; I had to set this explicitly because by default axios-retry conservatively only retries requests that are guaranteed to be idempotent, but in this case I needed to retry POSTs (and I know that in this context it's safe to do so).

I'm not sure which of these changes solved the problem or if they both helped, since I implemented them simultaneously. But I haven't seen any EPIPE or "socket hang up" errors since deploying the changes.

retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: Is there a way to detect VFP/NEON/Thumb/... on iOS at runtime? A:

First, consider carefully whether or not you really need to support armv6 binaries for iOS. According to published version share statistics, something like 98.5% of iOS devices are running iOS 5.0 or later, which does not support armv6 devices (armv6 binaries will still run on current iOS versions, obviously, but all new apps should really be targeting armv7; there’s basically zero reason for your customers to be shipping armv6 binaries for iOS today).

Similarly, your concerns about code size are misplaced. If you provide a fat library, and your customer builds an armv6 binary against it, only the armv6 bits of your library will be built into their application. Furthermore, code size is usually a nearly trivial fraction of application bundle size; most of the size of an application comes from other resources.

Ok. All that aside, if you really want to pursue this: VFP and thumb are supported on all iOS devices, so there’s no need to check for support. You can check for NEON and thumb-2 using the method that Eric Postpischil suggested (all armv7 iOS devices have NEON support, so availability of NEON coincides exactly with availability of thumb-2).

Liquibase provides a powerful mechanism for managing database migrations and supports SQL script execution with variable substitution. The situation you described involves Liquibase interpreting environment variables in SQL files that do not necessarily conform to the expected "LIQUIBASE_" prefix, which can lead to confusion.

### Explanation of Behavior

1. **Variable Substitution Mechanism**:
   - Liquibase allows the use of `${}` syntax for property substitution within changelogs, SQL files, and other resources. By default, it is designed to replace placeholders with values from various sources, primarily:
     - Values defined in the "liquibase.properties" file.
     - System properties (e.g., JVM properties).
     - Environment variables prefixed with "LIQUIBASE_".
     - Parameters passed directly to the Liquibase command.

2. **Actual Behavior**:
   - In your case, it appears that Liquibase is correctly replacing `${MY_VAR}` with `ABC` despite the absence of the "LIQUIBASE_" prefix.
   - According to the documentation, the replacement should prioritize variables with the "LIQUIBASE_" prefix, but if your implementation is replacing other variables as well, it could be due to unintended behavior or a bug in the Liquibase version you are using (4.20.0).

### Expected Behavior and Recommendations

- **Standard vs. Custom Handling**: Typically, the expectation is that only variables prefixed with "LIQUIBASE_" should be substituted. Any other variables not conforming to this prefix might not be reliably processed. If you find that other variables are inconsistently replaced, it might require further investigation, as this could suggest unexpected side effects or overrides in your Liquibase configuration or even within the environment.

- **Using Contexts and Labels**: If you have complex scenarios involving multiple environments and variable substitution, consider using **contexts** and **labels** as well. This will allow you to control which changelogs and changesets are activated based on specific conditions (e.g., environment) and help maintain clear boundaries for variable substitution.

### Troubleshooting Steps

1. **Review Configuration**: Check your `liquibase.properties` file, command-line parameters, and other configurations for any overrides that may influence variable resolution.

2. **Update Liquibase**: Ensure that you are using the latest stable version of Liquibase, as bugs and unexpected behaviors are often fixed in newer releases.

3. **Logs and Debugging**: Run Liquibase with increased logging (e.g., using `--logLevel=debug`), which can provide insights into how variables are processed.

4. **Test Environment Variables**: Create isolated tests for various variable names to verify behavior. Check if specific patterns (like the absence of the `LIQUIBASE_` prefix) consistently lead to either successful or unsuccessful substitutions.

5. **Documentation Review**: Continuously refer to Liquibase documentation and any release notes for potential changes related to property substitution.

### Conclusion

In summary, while Liquibase does prioritize environment variables prefixed with "LIQUIBASE_", your experience suggests some inconsistencies in handling other variable names. Ensure your configurations are sound, investigate specific behaviors with logs, and consider upgrading if you encounter lingering issues. If the behavior continues to be perplexing, it might be worth reaching out to the Liquibase community or checking open issues on their GitHub repository to see if others have encountered similar behavior.

In designing a RESTful API, the choice between using query parameters (e.g., `GET http://apibaseurl?city=sunnyvale`) and path parameters (e.g., `GET http://apibaseurl/city/sunnyvale`) is largely about semantic clarity, flexibility, and the nature of the resource being represented. Here’s a breakdown of the considerations and potential design advantages for using query parameters for a "city" in a weather forecast API:

### 1. **Semantic Clarity**

Using query parameters can make it clear that the information being requested is optional, meaning the client can specify different criteria for filtering. In contrast, a URI path implies a more resource-oriented retrieval. 

- **Query Parameters:** Indicates that the parameter is primarily for filtering or searching. This is appropriate for parameters like "city", where there can be multiple cities queried, potentially alongside other filters (like date, units, etc.).
  
- **Path Parameters:** Suggests that the resource being accessed is a specific entity. If you were accessing a specific city databasically as its unique resource, then using a path would be more appropriate.

### 2. **Flexibility in Queries**

The query parameter approach allows for easy addition of more search criteria without needing to modify the URI structure. For instance, if you want to add the ability to filter results by country or state, it can easily be done as follows:

- `GET http://apibaseurl?city=sunnyvale&country=us`

This is less straightforward with a path structure, which might require additional sub-paths or complicate the URI structure.

### 3. **Conformance to REST Principles**

According to RESTful principles, APIs should leverage statelessness and resource URIs. Query parameters are commonly used to represent non-hierarchical data (like filters, sorts, etc.) which maintains the RESTful abstraction of resources. Meanwhile, paths are more suited for hierarchical resource representations.

### 4. **Convenience for Client Implementation**

From a client perspective, building a request with query parameters can often be more straightforward and requires less stringent formatting. It also allows for easier URL parameterization when crafting requests based on user inputs (for instance, a search form).

### 5. **Consistent with Existing Usage**

As you noted, many existing APIs (like Yahoo Weather or OpenWeather) use query parameters for city names. Consistency within the ecosystem can reduce the learning curve for developers who are accustomed to working with such APIs and can help prevent confusion.

### Conclusion

While both methods can be valid within different contexts, using query parameters for search-related items like "city" often provides additional semantic clarity and flexibility. If your API is expected to grow and allow more query-like capabilities (like filtering by multiple fields), the query parameter approach is generally preferred. Path-based URIs are best reserved for when you are directly identifying and accessing a resource.

### Recommendation

If you decide to implement the query parameter approach, ensure that your API documentation is clear on how to use the API, including parameter options and structures to maintain ease of understanding for developers interfacing with your API.

Let's walk through the key elements of your setup to diagnose and propose a solution for your problem. ### Issue Overview You've stated that the anchor links for your recipes work correctly on your local server but change to a non-functional format when deployed. On deployment, the link appears like this: ``` http://thedeployedsserver.net/Home/Index/1?page=%2FRecipe ``` Instead of what you expected: ``` http://thedeployedsserver.net/Recipe/1 ``` This suggests that the routing for your Razor Pages is not resolving properly in your deployed environment. ### Possible Causes and Fixes 1. **Razor Page Route URL Format**: In Razor Pages, the route URL can depend on how you define the page routing. Given your `Recipe.cshtml` definition: ```csharp @page "{id}" ``` This informs ASP.NET Core that the page expects a single route parameter named `id`, which should be appended directly to the URL. **Fix**: Ensure that your page is located correctly at the root of a path that aligns with the routing you are expecting. If the `Recipe.cshtml` page is located in a folder, say `Pages/Recipes/`, then your link should reflect that: ```csharp

@recipe.Name

``` This adjustment ensures that the link aligns correctly with where the Razor page is located. 2. **Check Deployment Configuration**: Ensure that your deployment is properly configured to support your routing setup. For example, if you're using a web server (like IIS), ensure that the server is set up to handle the requests correctly and is configured to route requests to the ASP.NET Core application correctly. 3. **Static Files and MVC Configuration**: In your `Startup.cs` file: ```csharp app.UseMvcWithDefaultRoute(); ``` The `UseMvcWithDefaultRoute` call might override any routing setup for Razor Pages. You should use `app.UseEndpoints` to configure endpoint routing, especially if using .NET Core 3.0 or later: ```csharp public void Configure(IApplicationBuilder app, IHostingEnvironment env) { if (env.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage(); } app.UseAuthentication(); app.UseStaticFiles(); app.UseRouting(); // Important for endpoint routing app.UseAuthorization(); // Important for authorization app.UseEndpoints(endpoints => { endpoints.MapRazorPages(); // Map Razor Pages explicitly }); } ``` 4. **Clear Browser Cache or Server Cache**: Sometimes routes might be cached. Clear your browser cache or restart your application to see if the issue resolves. ### Summary of Action Items - Adjust your Razor Page navigation links to reflect the correct path. - Use endpoint routing in the `Startup.cs` as outlined above. - Ensure that your deployment environment mirrors your local configurations as closely as possible. title: Why is there no language support in C++ for all C++ standard library type traits?
ground_truth_answer:
There are many aspects of the C++ standard library which cannot be implemented without support from the compiler. For example, type_info. A "freestanding C++ library" implementation can't provide such a type, since it is the result of a keyword-based expression: typeid. The only people who could provide such a thing are compiler writers, since the compiler is the one who has to generate those objects.

The same is true of many other elements of the standard library. exception_ptr, current_exception(s), initializer_list, etc. There's a whole chapter of this stuff in the C++ standard.

Not all components of the standard library can be implemented without compiler support. Type traits are simply one more thing which a freestanding C++ library cannot implement. Not in ISO standard C++.

As for why they didn't provide the tools needed to implement them? Because that would have taken more time. Note that reflection isn't even a fully-formed TS yet, while type-traits have been standard for 5 years now.

It is difficult to specify general tools like reflection. To know exactly what behavior you need and how it should be provided. It's much easier to look at common usage patterns (as exemplified by Boost) and just use them. Type-traits are the low-hanging fruit of reflection.

Your question touches on some important aspects of C++ type traits and the relationship between the language and its standard library. Let's break it down:

### Why Some Type Traits Require Compiler Intrinsics

C++ type traits are a collection of templates that provide compile-time information about types. In the C++ standard library, traits like `std::is_trivially_destructible`, `std::is_trivially_copyable`, and similar traits depend on properties that are closely tied to the underlying implementation of the types and the compilation process itself. 

Unfortunately, some of these properties cannot be reliably determined through pure language constructs alone, especially in older standards. For instance, `std::is_trivially_destructible` deals with whether a type has a trivial destructor, which involves knowledge that the compiler must provide about the type's memory layout and the behavior of its destructor — knowledge not accessible merely through C++ syntax and semantics as defined in the standard.

Due to this, certain traits may require compiler intrinsics or specific implementation details that are not part of the standard C++ language. This leads to the necessity of falling back on compiler-specific features, which is a limitation of the current C++ type model.

### Language Support and Non-Standard Compiler Extensions

In essence, while the standard library provides a robust set of type traits, the expectation that all compilers must simply fulfill all type traits in a fully compliant manner is complicated by the need for some underlying compiler features. The standard must take into account various implementations across a wide range of compilers and platforms. 

In §17.6.1.3.2 of the standard, while it mandates the inclusion of `<type_traits>` in freestanding implementations, it does not explicitly define how certain traits can be implemented if they are inherently outside the capabilities of the language constructs themselves. This creates an expectation that compilers must go beyond standard compliance to reliably provide all features defined in `<type_traits>`. 

### Why Were Such Traits Allowed in the Standard?

This decision might stem from several reasons:

1. **Evolution of C++**: The language and its features have evolved over time. Initially, certain traits were added as compiler technology advanced, and the C++ standards committee sought to provide capabilities that reflected modern programming patterns.
   
2. **Pragmatic Approach**: The committee may have opted for a pragmatic approach to type traits knowing that many modern compilers would support them as they become increasingly sophisticated.

3. **Cross-Compatibility**: The committee aimed to ensure compatibility and usability across different platforms and compilers. By defining traits abstractly in standardization, the committee allows compilers room to implement them according to their capabilities, thus promoting a wider range of compliance.

### Fixing the Problem 

1. **Feature Detection**: For situations where a trait might not be available, as hinted in the references, one could implement feature detection to determine if the C++ standard library is providing the trait. By using tag dispatching or SFINAE (Substitution Failure Is Not An Error), you can implement a fallback mechanism to use alternative means (like `std::has_trivial_destructor`) when a trait isn't available.

2. **Understanding Compiler Limitations**: If you’re targeting older compilers that do not have modern type traits, you might need to check the availability of certain traits with techniques like preprocessor directives, similar to what was mentioned in the references. This way, you can ensure your code remains portable across various compiler versions.

### Conclusion

While C++ type traits are an essential tool for template programming and type introspection, some of them necessitate compiler support that goes beyond standard language features. This presents challenges regarding compliance and portability. Understanding these limitations and utilizing techniques such as feature detection can aid in writing more robust C++ code that is less dependent on compiler-specific extensions.

title: Auto Creating a Table in SQL
ground_truth_answer:
Based on my experience, It's highly not recommendable to create each table for each user because it's very expensive in terms of space and resources. If Facebook were doing the same thing, they would be having 1.1 billion tables on their database! Instead of that they have 1 table for all these members. Use one table, then keep a Primary Key column e.g. Id to be used to identify the person. e.g. 

$sql = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
          id INT(10) NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
          names VARCHAR(100),
          email VARCHAR(100),
          password VARCHAR(200)
        )";
mysql_query($sql) or die(mysql_error());

Then as user signs up, the id column auto increments, thus he/she will have a unique Id that you can use to trace him/her, like this;

$res = mysql_query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id ='".$id."'") or die(mysql_error());
$data = mysql_fetch_assoc($res);
echo $data['names']." ".$data['email']; /* names, email, password ... etc */

This is much better. Rather than creating 1 million tables, you can just have 1 table for all the 1 million people.

Regards!

retrieved_context.question_title: How to develop a simple database
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: How to develop a simple database A:

Simple interface does not always imply simple software (just a friendly word of caution).

Your program will end up being event-driven (e.g. "do this when this button is clicked") as opposed to procedural, so you will definitely be on a learning curve in that respect. You will be forced to learn new ways of handling your data (procedural code can just pass data forwards, while event-driven software will often need to access things in more or less random order). This is where database software can help. It separates your data from your code.

Using a database such as MySQL is quite nice, especially compared to creating your own database, which would be reinventing the wheel in this case. Most database software will handle what you're looking to do quite well (and several are free, including MySQL).

I'd suggest starting off with some simple "get to know MySQL" programs to get used to querying, inserting, etc. There are several excellent tutorials online (W3 Schools has one).

When learning how to use a database effectively it pays to really plan out everything you'd like it to store, e.g. name, birthday, address, phone#. You'll likely have to reconstruct your database table(s) a few times while you learn what works and what doesn't.

If you're not on a deadline this is an excellent learning opportunity!

To address the question about the best HTML tag for labeling information that is not within a form, you're correct in noting that the `<label>` tag is specifically designated for form controls. When you want to represent name-value pairs outside of a form, a good semantic choice is to use a **definition list**, which is made up of `<dl>`, `<dt>`, and `<dd>` tags.

Here's how you could structure your data using a definition list:

```html
<dl>
    <dt>Name</dt>
    <dd>John</dd>
    <dt>Age</dt>
    <dd>40</dd>
    <dt>City</dt>
    <dd>Frankfurt</dd>
    <dt>Country</dt>
    <dd>Germany</dd>
    <dt>Status</dt>
    <dd>Active</dd>
</dl>

<hr />

<dl>
    <dt>Name</dt>
    <dd>Maria</dd>
    <dt>Age</dt>
    <dd>30</dd>
    <dt>City</dt>
    <dd>Bonn</dd>
    <dt>Country</dt>
    <dd>Germany</dd>
    <dt>Status</dt>
    <dd>Inactive</dd>
</dl>
```

### Explanation:
- **`<dl>`**: This represents a definition list, a container for a list of terms and their descriptions.
- **`<dt>`** (definition term): This is used for the term being defined, which would be "Name", "Age", etc.
- **`<dd>`** (definition description): This provides the description or value corresponding to the term, such as "John", "40", etc.

**Advantages of Using `<dl>`:**
1. **Semantic Meaning**: Using a definition list provides clear semantics for the relationship between the term (label) and its description (value).
2. **Accessibility**: Screen readers can interpret the structure of a definition list, helping visually impaired users understand the relationship between terms and their corresponding descriptions.
3. **Consistency**: If you have multiple pieces of information structured in this way on the same page, it's easy to maintain and intuitive to understand.

### When to Use `<strong>`:
You mentioned using `<strong>` tags for emphasizing importance. The `<strong>` tag does convey importance but lacks the semantic clarity needed in this context, especially since it does not indicate a label-description relationship.

### Conclusion:
Using a definition list (`<dl>`, `<dt>`, and `<dd>`) is the best practice for your situation, as it clearly categorizes the information while remaining semantically correct in the context of HTML. This approach is especially effective for displaying multiple sets of related information, maintaining clarity and structure across the document.

<mx:Panel dropShadowVisible="false" ...>

If you can't access the property directly and you are getting compilation errors, consider checking any styles that might default to using a shadow. You might want to explicitly set them to their default states.

<mx:Panel styleName="yourCustomPanelStyle" ...>

If the `dropShadowVisible` property isn't an option, another approach would be to replace the `Panel` component with an alternative component that doesn’t rely on that property. For example, you could use a `Group` or `VGroup` to create a similar layout without the drop shadow application.

### 4. Update Your Library References
Sometimes such issues can arise from the usage of older versions or mismatched references in your project. Ensure that you are using the latest versions of any libraries or components you depend upon and that they are compatible with the Flex SDK version you are using.

The most straightforward approach is to use the `dropShadowVisible` property if available in your context. retrieved_context.question_title: What is the most pythonic way to structure a multi-module python program?
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: What is the most pythonic way to structure a multi-module python program? A:

Modules that need to access each other's namespace is not the same as modules that need to share the same namespace. I can't think of anything you can do with from modulename import * that you can't do with import modulename. You just have to preface a lot of your names with modulename. That's a good thing, not a bad thing. It makes your code self-documenting, which is why from modulename import * is to be avoided.

You can have the UI and main flow modules import each other. The only way you'll run into problems is if you reference names between them outside of the scope of functions. For example

# mainflow.py
import ui # interpreter stops reading mainflow and starts reading ui

class Foo:
    ...

theUI = ui.UI()

# ui.py
import mainflow # mainflow already being loaded; interpretation of ui continues uninterrupted

def dosomething():
    myfoo = mainflow.Foo() # so far so good, not interpreted until the function is called

class Bar(mainflow.Foo): # mainflow.Foo not reached yet, error here
    ...

class UI:
    ...

On the other hand if ui happens to get imported first, then you get the error at theUI = ui.UI(), when all of mainflow has been interpreted but ui has only been interpreted as far as import mainflow. As long as you put all the references to each other inside functions, though, you can get along fine. E.g.

# mainflow.py
import ui
...

To resolve the issue of importing modules in your Python package `bpt` both when it's run as a standalone application and when it's nested within another project (`brain_seg`), you can consider the following approach.

### Current Problem
1. When you run `run.py` from `bpt`, the imports like `import module1` and `import module2` work fine because Python recognizes them in the same namespace.
2. When `bpt` is nested under `brain_seg`, the import statements fail since Python looks for `module1` and `module2` in the global namespace where they don't exist, leading to a `ModuleNotFoundError`.
3. Attempting to use relative imports (`from . import module1`) works in the nested context, but causes issues when executing directly from `bpt`, leading to an `ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package`.

### Proposed Solution
The best approach is to manage imports in a way that allows both standalone and nested execution without throwing errors. Here’s how you can achieve that:

1. **Modify the Import Statements in `run.py`:**
   Use a combination of condition checks to determine the context in which the script is running.

```python
import os

# Check if the script is being run as the main module
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Importing as standalone
    import module1
    import module2
else:
    # Importing as a submodule
    from . import module1
    from . import module2

# Your existing code logic below...
```

### Explanation:
- The `if __name__ == "__main__":` check allows you to run the modules in the standalone context. When `run.py` is executed directly, it will import `module1` and `module2` from the same directory.
- If `run.py` is loaded as part of a module (like in `brain_seg`), the `else` block will trigger, and it will import `module1` and `module2` relative to the package structure.

### Running the Project:
1. To run `bpt` standalone:
   ```bash
   python path/to/bpt/run.py
   ```
   This will execute the `run.py` script, and the standalone imports will work as expected.

2. To run `run.py` as part of `brain_seg`:
   ```bash
   python -m brain_seg.bpt.run
   ```
   This will treat the directory as a package, enabling the relative imports.

### Additional Tips:
- Make sure your project structure is clear, and you have an `__init__.py` in the necessary directories to make them packages. While you may have been following this, it's crucial for Python to recognize the directories as modules.
- Always test both ways of running your modules to ensure that import paths resolve correctly under different conditions.

This approach gives you flexibility while maintaining the readability of your imports. It also prevents potential circular import issues when the modules might refer to each other.

This isn't a good answer to your question, but I think it will save you some work. There are going to be some issues with the app you describe. As a spin-off of @hsander's ideas, you could have the user take a picture of a nearby store's sign/logo and use image processing (e.g. Google Goggles) to match it and figure out where the user is. If you have a budget and ability to install things in the mall, you could put GPS antennas on the roof of the mall in different places and then use a repeater to broadcast the signal inside the mall. My company has a setup like this, and I get impeccable GPS while indoors. You would be able to know which repeater the user is closer to by their GPS coordinates and direct them accordingly.

In terms of display, you can use simple View or SurfaceView to display a map floorplan. Using a map-related API is probably going to be overkill and it will be even less useful without user's location. I suggest for calculating shortest path, you create a graph and use Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm. You could use Google maps to help you create a node graph with real distances

This is a clever idea, but I think you may come into some difficulty when going for precision and accuracy here, since it is NOT ONLY DISTANCE from an access point but actually A MULTITUDE of factors which determines signal strength. For instance, the location in the room as compared with a large bookshelf, or a television, might influence one of the signals more strongly than the others. Even the position of your body with respect to the device might disrupt the signal.

I suggest trying some feature selection techniques and/or some other learning algorithms which can hone in better on which dimensions in your data are giving you the most consistent information. For example, simple statistical analysis can tell you the mean and standard deviation of signal strength of each signal from within a given "location". Then you can compare locations' statistics, and see if you have statistically significant differences in any of these signals across locations. You may want to consider the following tests:

  • T-test is like ANOVA but just for comparing pairs of locations

retrieved_context.question_title: Why do all devices discovered by CBCentralmanager have name=null?
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
Q: Why do all devices discovered by CBCentralmanager have name=null? A:

Not all devices advertise their name. There is very little space in an advertising packet (~30 bytes), and the name may not fit if there are other more-important things to advertise. A single custom service can use up 16 bytes. You may not be able to determine the name without connecting. Even then, the device may not have a BLE name.

I would normally have expected the console to show nearby discoverable devices as well as already-connected devices.

I'm not sure why you expect that. scanForPeripherals returns information about devices that are advertising. It is very common for a device to stop advertising when it's connected to (it's common for devices to only support a single connection). If you want to see connected devices, call retrieveConnectedPeripherals.

Locating other users of your app in real-time, similar to how Venmo or other location-based services operate, can be a complex task in iOS, particularly with the limitations and functionalities available in iOS 7. Here’s a breakdown of the steps and considerations you'll need to take into account:

### 1. Using Location Services
To find nearby users, you will likely integrate location services:

- **Core Location Framework**: iOS offers the Core Location framework, which allows the app to get the user’s current location. You can obtain the latitude and longitude coordinates, which are essential for geographically locating users.

- **Requesting Permissions**: Ensure that you request the proper permissions to use location services. Starting from iOS 8, you need to define keys in your `Info.plist` file (such as `NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription` or `NSLocationAlwaysUsageDescription`) to prompt the user for location access.

### 2. Server-Side Logic for User Tracking
Real-time communication between users will require a server:

- **Backend Service**: You will need a backend to handle user registrations and store their locations. Each time a user's location is updated, the app would send this information to your server.

- **Database**: Use a database to store user coordinates (latitude and longitude) alongside a timestamp.

### 3. Real-Time Updates
To efficiently get the locations of nearby users:

- **WebSocket or Push Notification Services**: Implement a real-time communication channel using WebSockets or similar technology to notify users of nearby people dynamically.

- **Geofencing**: You could implement geofencing, where the server calculates if another user falls within a defined radius from the requestor’s location.

### 4. Finding Nearby Users
With users' location data available on your server, you can find nearby users:

- **Distance Calculation**: You will need to calculate the distance between the current user and others using the Haversine formula or similar methods based on their coordinates.

- **Radius Filtering**: Establish a radius (for example, 1 km) and filter users who are within that distance.

### 5. Privacy Considerations
It's crucial to prioritize user privacy:

- **User Consent**: Always ensure that users give explicit consent to share their location and are aware of who can see their information.

- **Anonymization**: You might consider anonymizing user location data or allowing them to toggle the visibility ("I am available" mode).

### 6. Example Implementation Flow
Here’s a high-level implementation flow:

1. **User opens app**: App requests location permissions.
2. **Location fetched**: Use Core Location to fetch user's current location.
3. **Send Location to Server**: Send the user's location and any other identifier to your backend regularly or when there’s a significant change.
4. **Server processes locations**: Upon receipt, update this user's location in your database.
5. **Finding near users**: Whenever the app needs to find nearby users, query the database for user locations within the specified radius.
6. **Display Results**: Return the results to the app and display them to the user.

### 7. Alternative Technologies
- **Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)**: For very private scenarios (like payments in close range), BLE can be efficient. However, it is limited to short distances and requires the Bluetooth to be enabled on both devices.
  
- **Third-Party Libraries**: Consider using third-party services (like the ones mentioned in your references) that might simplify this process, focusing on user location and nearby discovery.

By taking a combination of these approaches, you should be able to build a solid feature for locating nearby users within your app while considering privacy and efficiency. If you want to create a seamless experience akin to Venmo's, the crucial element would be the real-time data handling and user permission management.

title: Catching an exception from the setTimeout function executed inside an instance of a Promise object
ground_truth_answer:
After some discussions and comments, my task was solved by this approach:

const someFunction = timeout => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, timeout));

someFunction(timeout).then(() => doSomething()).catch(() => console.log(`This code will not be executed`));

If an exception occurs in an asynchronous function:

someFunction(timeout).then(ErrorEvent).catch(() => console.log(`This code will not be executed`));

Such solutions are still possible:

const testF = () => { throw new Error(`Упс! Бросили исключение.`) }

const genPromise = () => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
        try {
            const res = testF()
            resolve(res)
        } catch (e) { reject(e) }
    }, 1e3)
})

t1: {
    const log = console.log.bind(console, 't1:')
    const _then = log.bind(console, 'then:')
    const _catch = log.bind(console, 'catch:')

    genPromise()
        .then(_then)
        .catch(_catch)
        .then(_then)
}

t2: {
    const log = console.log.bind(console, 't2:')
    const _then = log.bind(console, 'then:')
    const _catch = log.bind(console, 'catch:')

    void async function () {
        let pRes = null
        try {
            pRes = await genPromise()
        } catch (e) {
            _catch(e.message)
        }
        _then(pRes)
    }()
}

retrieved_context.question_title: How promise chains reference the next error handler
retrieved_context.chunk_text:
objects aren't equal.

Now what happens if we wait a bit and then attach a new catch handler to p?

setTimeout(() => p.catch(console.log), 500)

You should notice another console log, this time with only 'Hi from p!'

And the reason is order at which a Promise evaluates. It evaluates on creation and if it's created on a rejected promise, it evaluates to rejected and goes to the catch handler.

What do you think you'll get with the following?

Promise
  .reject(new Error('1'))
  .catch(console.log)
  .then(() => Promise.reject(new Error('2')))
  .then(() => new Error('3'))
  .then(console.log)
  .catch(console.log)
  .catch(() => console.log('4'))

That's right you'll see a printed Error('1'), then a printed Error('2'), but not a printed Error('3') or a printed '4'. That's because a .catch promise does one of two things: resolves the promise to the resolved value, or resolves the promise to the functions value if the chain is rejected.

In contrast .then only resolves a promise. If it's resolution is rejected, it rejects with the resolution.

It's a little confusing yes, but once you realize that promise will wait for resolution and will check and chaining promises it becomes a little easier to figure out where you'll reject to.

The problem you described, where Word 2007 displays the "Getting list of available content types..." dialog indefinitely when trying to save documents to a SharePoint 2007 (MOSS) document library, is a known issue that can have a few underlying causes. Here’s a comprehensive approach to address this issue:

### 1. **Check for Updates** 
Since you mentioned that this issue has been acknowledged by Microsoft and was targeted to be fixed in a Cumulative Update (CU), ensure that your SharePoint installation is updated to the latest cumulative updates and service packs. Applying the latest updates can resolve many operational bugs and performance issues.

### 2. **Content Types Configuration**
Given that the document libraries are customized and deployed using features in a solution, verify the content type configuration:
- **Ensure Content Type Association**: Confirm that the content types are correctly associated with the document libraries. Sometimes, if the content types are not properly linked, Word may struggle to fetch them.
- **Default Content Type**: It’s advisable to have a universally recognized content type (like the standard Document content type) set as the default in the document library. 

### 3. **User Permissions**
Check if the user has the appropriate permissions to access the content types. Insufficient permissions can lead to delays or failures when querying for content types. Verify roles and permissions for the users experiencing the issue.

### 4. **Performance Monitoring**
While you indicated that resource usage is under control, monitor performance closely to ensure:
- **Check SQL Server Availability**: Ensure SQL Server is responsive and the databases are healthy. Use SQL Server Management Studio to monitor performance and check for any locks or issues.
- **Networking Issues**: Since this is happening in a medium server farm, check the network latency between the application server and the SQL server, as well as any potential firewall or network settings that might be affecting communication.

### 5. **Client Configuration**
Configuration on the client (Word 2007) may also impact behavior:
- **Repair Office Installation**: Perform a "Repair" on the Microsoft Office installation, which can fix any corrupted components causing the problem.
- **Clear Office Cache**: Clear out any cached files by navigating to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Office\`, and deleting or renaming the “Office file cache” folder when Word is closed.

### 6. **Check ULS Logs**
Since you're on SharePoint 2007, reviewing the ULS logs can provide insights into what might be happening when the dialog hangs. Look for any specific error messages or warnings that might correlate with the user’s actions in Word. 

### 7. **Alternative Save As Option**
As a temporary workaround, users can save the document locally and then manually upload it to SharePoint. This can alleviate immediate frustration until a more permanent solution (like applying the update) is in place.

### 8. **Consult Community and Microsoft**
Keep an eye on discussions in SharePoint community forums, as other users may have similar experiences. Additionally, depending on your support agreement with Microsoft, you may want to follow up on your existing case to ensure you are informed of any patches or other solutions that are being released.

By investigating the above points, you should either resolve the issue or narrow down its root cause. If the issue persists after taking these steps, further assistance may be needed, potentially involving Microsoft support for a deeper diagnosis.

title: Registering application in windows registry
ground_truth_answer:
Yes there are multiple places in the registry where you can put application information and which key to use depends on what/why you are registering.

I would argue that the main registration point is the registration for "Default Programs" under SOFTWARE\RegisteredApplications. If your application fits one of the client types then you should point your RegisteredApplications value to Software\Clients\%ClientType%\%YourCanonicalName%\Capabilities, otherwise you can use any key like Software\%YourCompany%\%YourApp%\Capabilities or Software\Classes\Applications\%Filename%\Capabilities.

If you want your application to appear in the "Open With" dialog of a specific file extension then you can list your ProgId under HKCR\%.ext%\OpenWithProgids or the application filename under HKCR\%.ext%\OpenWithList.

General "Open With" information is stored under HKCR\Applications\%Filename%.

The Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\App Paths key is mainly used as a %Path% environment variable extension for the shell so it can find the full path to your executable if the user types just the filename in the Run dialog. When it comes to registering applications in the Windows Registry, Microsoft provides various paths, each serving different purposes and scenarios. Here's a breakdown of the paths you mentioned, along with the reasons for choosing one over another:

1. **HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\App Paths\MyApp.exe**
   
   This registry path is used primarily to register the application executable, allowing Windows to locate and execute the application from anywhere in the system using just its filename (e.g., running `MyApp.exe` from the Run dialog). When you create a subkey for your application under this path, you typically set a default value that points to the full path of the executable file. This is beneficial for user-specific configurations. If multiple users on a system use the application, this key will provide a personalized reference for the user currently logged in.

   **Use Case**: This path is ideal when you want to facilitate easy access to your application through Run commands, shortcuts, or when it is called from scripts. 

2. **HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Classes\MyApp**
   
   This key is used for registering the application with custom file types or protocols. When you create a key under `Classes`, you can define how your application interacts with specific file types (for example, associating `.myext` files with `MyApp`). This is often accompanied by additional values that help specify file associations, icons, and more.

   **Use Case**: Use this key when you're creating file associations so that double-clicking a file of your type opens your application directly. 

3. **HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Classes\Applications\MyApp.exe**
   
   This key is typically used for application registration tailored to file associations or to provide necessary information to the shell regarding the application. It can contain additional data specific to the application, such as `FriendlyAppName`, `Icon`, and others that enhance integration into the Windows environment.

   **Use Case**: When you want to provide shell integration details, set application icons, or specify other shell-related attributes for a registered executable, it's helpful to use this path.

### Differences and Scenarios for Choosing One Over Another:

- **Path Resolution**: 
  - `App Paths` is primarily for resolving the executable's path, allowing users to run the app from anywhere without needing a full path.
  - Classes keys deal more with file-type associations, which are necessary for integrating the app with Windows File Explorer.

- **Functionality**:
  - Using `App Paths` is suitable for a straightforward application execution scenario while the Classes paths (both `Classes` and `Applications`) are more intricate, offering greater control over file-type handling and interactions with the system.

- **Occupancy**:
  - You may find that some applications primarily use the `Classes` registry paths because they focus on providing associations with file types rather than just making the executable readily accessible.

### Recommendations:

- If your application needs to be executed easily via command prompts or Run dialogs, definitely use the `App Paths` key to ensure users can find and run your application without an absolute path.

- If your application handles specific types of files (for example, a text editor for `.txt` files), ensure to register those types under `Classes`.

- If you need to clarify the behavior of your executable within the Windows ecosystem (like adding custom icons or setting specific flags for application features), make use of the `Applications` key.

### Conclusion

Ultimately, the choice between these registry paths depends on how the application is intended to be used and integrated into the Windows operating system. It is common for applications to utilize multiple registry paths to achieve various functionalities—like running the application itself, associating file types, and integrating with Windows Explorer features. Thus, it's not necessarily wrong if different applications appear to primarily register under different paths; the application design and user experience will dictate the optimal choice.

Make sure your Visual Studio 2013 is updated to the latest version. You can check for updates from within Visual Studio:

- Go to **Tools** > **Extensions and Updates**.
- In the **Updates** tab, check for any available updates for Visual Studio itself or any installed components.

### 3. Ensure Correct Component Installation

Sometimes, certain components of SSDT may not be installed properly. Follow these steps:

- Re-run the SSDT installation process. During the installation, ensure that the options for SQL Server Database Projects are checked.

title: How to populate a DataGridViewCombobBoxColumn with values
ground_truth_answer:
The first thing you need to explain is why you have your column set to be a checkboxcolumn and not a comboboxcolumn? That may be your whole problem.

Now, by your code, you have a list already filled with your possible industries. How are you going to databind to any of your tuples(rows) if you don't have any rows to begin with? You should be databinding all of the cells in the column after you fill your dgv with your query result.

If that's not the issue I made a simple example of databinding a List<String> to a cell.

Here's an example of putting a List into a datagridviewcombobox:

    private List<String> theList = new List<String>();
    public Form1()
    {
        InitializeComponent();
        theList.Add("is");
        theList.Add("this");
        theList.Add("working");
        theList.Add("yet?");
        DataGridViewComboBoxCell dropDown = (DataGridViewComboBoxCell) dgv.Rows[0].Cells[0];
        dropDown.DataSource = theList;

    }

    private void aButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        theList.Clear();
        theList.Add("I");
        theList.Add("Knew");
        theList.Add("this");
        theList.Add("would");
        theList.Add("work!!!");
    }

How can I avoid doing another pass to set the correct values?

You can't (maybe). The datagridview is going to load one result at a time. Unless you are returning multiple values for that one cell, you are going to have to do another pass. The dgv is expecting to fill in the row with the data its given for that particular row. What you can try is not recognizing that column exists in your query (just remove it from the query) and that may cause it to pass over that column and not assign it a value. If that succeeds what you have to do next is make that cell automatically be those values when the row is created. You will know this is working if you were to just add rows and those cells were immediately populated even though there's no other data in any of the cells.

Why do I need to first load the rows and only then bind the datasource? This seems rather unintuitive and it causes my problem. What if the requirements ask for more data to be loaded at some point after the initial load? Would I then need to do the binding again?

You have to have an object to databind to. Databinding to the column won't make you databind to the cells in that column. It wouldn't even databind to the column header. You have to databind to the cells themselves. Once you databind, you can change that list as much as you want and the cells which are databinded to your list will change as well. Once you understand this concept databinding will be a lot easier to implement in the future.

Looking at your code again I suggest you create your columns before you fill your table with data. That way your dgv doesn't skip the creation of the column when you insert your results, but skips the data allotment for that column. In your foreach loop create a row, assign the data, databind the cell to your List<String> and add the row to your datagridview. Once that's all working go grab yourself a drink and pat yourself on the back for a job well done.

Edit

Instead of doing what I previously said, try this. It doesn't even involve databinding a list. If you know what your string values are going to be for your drop down box at design time you can go to Columns>your_column>Items and enter the strings there. If you don't, that's ok too. Whenever you have your list of strings you can add them to the column's internal list like so:

    foo DataGridViewComboBoxColumn = myDGV.columns("YourColumn")
    foo.Items.Add("blarggg")

If you need to change the list at any time, all rows will be updated upon making said change.

Very briefly, pointer events has 3 main drawbacks relative to the alternative:

1) Mobile-first web: Pointer events would likely never supplant touch events on the web (especially without support from Safari). Since touch events are here to stay, supporting another largely redundant input model has a high long-term complexity cost on the web platform.

2) Performance: The hit testing model required by pointer events imposes a non-trivial performance penalty (hit test on every movement event) that neither Android, iOS or touch events has.
